---
title: "TLS, certificates and trust"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

zuhttp does not ship cryptography or a list of trusted certificate
authorities. It uses the TLS implementation and the trust store your
operating system already has: Schannel and the Windows certificate store on
Windows, Apple's TLS and the Keychain on macOS, and OpenSSL with the system CA
directory elsewhere. A certificate your organisation installs on its machines
is trusted by zuhttp with no configuration, and an OS security update reaches
zuhttp without a new release.

The price is that behaviour follows the platform. This article shows what you
can configure, and how zuhttp tells you — rather than quietly doing less —
when a platform cannot do what you asked.

```{r setup}
library(zuhttp)
zu_tls_backend()
```

This article was built with the backend above; what it supports is reported
by `zu_info()`:

```{r caps}
zu_info()$tls_capabilities
```

## A local HTTPS server

To show trust decisions without depending on the internet, the examples use a
local HTTPS server ([webfakes](https://webfakes.r-lib.org)) with a
certificate from a certificate authority created just for this article.

<details><summary>Creating the throwaway certificate authority</summary>

```{r certs}
ssl <- function(...) system2("openssl", c(...), stdout = FALSE, stderr = FALSE)
d <- tempfile("zuhttp-tls-"); dir.create(d)
f <- function(x) file.path(d, x)

# A certificate authority...
ssl("req", "-x509", "-newkey", "rsa:2048", "-nodes", "-days", "30",
    "-keyout", f("ca.key"), "-out", f("ca.pem"), "-subj", "/CN=article-CA")
# ...and a server certificate it signs, valid for the name "localhost" only.
writeLines(c("subjectAltName=DNS:localhost", "basicConstraints=CA:FALSE",
             "keyUsage=digitalSignature,keyEncipherment",
             "extendedKeyUsage=serverAuth"), f("leaf.ext"))
ssl("req", "-newkey", "rsa:2048", "-nodes", "-keyout", f("leaf.key"),
    "-out", f("leaf.csr"), "-subj", "/CN=localhost")
ssl("x509", "-req", "-in", f("leaf.csr"), "-CA", f("ca.pem"), "-CAkey", f("ca.key"),
    "-CAcreateserial", "-days", "30", "-extfile", f("leaf.ext"), "-out", f("leaf.pem"))
writeLines(c(readLines(f("leaf.pem")), readLines(f("leaf.key"))), f("server.pem"))

free_port <- function() {
  repeat {
    p <- sample(20000:40000, 1)
    s <- try(serverSocket(p), silent = TRUE)
    if (!inherits(s, "try-error")) { close(s); return(p) }
  }
}
port <- free_port()
srv <- webfakes::new_app_process(
  webfakes::httpbin_app(), port = paste0(port, "s"),
  opts = webfakes::server_opts(remote = TRUE, ssl_certificate = f("server.pem")),
  start = TRUE
)
```

</details>

```{r urls}
site <- sprintf("https://localhost:%d/get", port)   # the name on the certificate
ca   <- f("ca.pem")                                 # the authority that signed it
```

## Verification is on, and cannot be half-off

A certificate from an authority the system does not trust is refused, and
the condition says why:

```{r untrusted}
e <- tryCatch(zu_get(site), error = function(e) e)
class(e)[1:2]
conditionMessage(e)
```

The classes separate the causes, because the fixes differ: an unknown issuer
is `zu_tls_certificate_error`, a certificate for a different name is
`zu_tls_hostname_error`, and a failed negotiation is `zu_tls_handshake_error`.
All are `zu_tls_error`.

## Trusting your own certificate authority

Two settings, deliberately different:

- `ca_extra` **adds** an authority to the system store. The system's
  authorities are still trusted. This is the usual choice: an internal CA
  alongside the public internet.
- `ca_file` **replaces** the system store. *Only* the authorities in the file
  are trusted, and every public site will fail.

```{r ca}
r <- zu_get(site, tls = zu_tls(ca_extra = ca))
zu_resp_status(r)

r <- zu_get(site, tls = zu_tls(ca_file = ca))
zu_resp_status(r)
```

Both succeed here, because this server is signed by the one authority either
setting trusts. The difference shows on any other site: with `ca_file`, a
public host that verified a moment ago now fails. The printed configuration
spells out which one you have:

```{r ca-print}
zu_tls(ca_extra = ca)
```

Put the setting on a client to apply it to every request:

```{r ca-client}
internal <- zu_client(tls = zu_tls(ca_extra = ca))
zu_resp_status(zu_get(site, client = internal))
```

`ca_file` and `ca_extra` are not available on Windows yet; there they raise
`zu_tls_unsupported_error` rather than falling back to the system store.

### Certificate files: `.crt`, `.cer`, `.pem`

Both settings take the path to a certificate file, whatever its extension —
your IT department's `corporate-root.crt` works as it is, provided it is in
**PEM** format: text, starting with `-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----`. A file may
hold several certificates one after another (a bundle), and each is used.

```{r crt}
crt <- f("corporate-root.crt")
invisible(file.copy(ca, crt))
readLines(crt, n = 1)
zu_resp_status(zu_get(site, tls = zu_tls(ca_extra = crt)))
```

The same extension is also used for **DER**, a binary encoding, and a
certificate exported from the Windows certificate manager as `.cer` often is.
zuhttp reads PEM only and says so, with the command that converts it:

```{r der, error = TRUE}
der <- f("corporate-root-der.crt")
ssl("x509", "-in", ca, "-outform", "der", "-out", der)
zu_get(site, tls = zu_tls(ca_extra = der))
```


## The name must match

The certificate names `localhost`. The same server reached as `127.0.0.1` is
refused, even with the authority trusted, because a valid certificate for a
different name proves nothing about this one:

```{r hostname}
by_ip <- sprintf("https://127.0.0.1:%d/get", port)
e <- tryCatch(zu_get(by_ip, tls = zu_tls(ca_extra = ca)), error = function(e) e)
class(e)[1]
```

## What was negotiated

```{r connection}
r <- zu_get(site, client = internal)
str(zu_resp_connection(r)[c("tls_protocol", "tls_cipher", "trust_backend")])
```

`trust_backend` names the store that vouched for the certificate. It is
reported separately from the protocol because on macOS the two are different
frameworks.

## Asking for more: refused, never downgraded

Every `zu_tls()` setting asks for a *stronger* connection. When the platform
cannot provide one, zuhttp raises `zu_tls_unsupported_error` before
connecting, instead of connecting without it. This loop asks for each setting
on the platform that built this page:

```{r refusals}
settings <- list(
  pins       = zu_tls(pins = "sha256//AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA="),
  tls13      = zu_tls(min_version = 13, ca_extra = ca),
  revocation = zu_tls(revocation = TRUE, ca_extra = ca)
)
for (nm in names(settings)) {
  res <- tryCatch(zu_resp_status(zu_get(site, tls = settings[[nm]])),
                  error = function(e) class(e)[1])
  cat(format(nm, width = 11), res, "\n")
}
```

Where a setting is supported you see a status or a verification error; where
it is not, `zu_tls_unsupported_error`, and no connection was attempted. The
pin above is deliberately wrong, so a platform that pins reports
`zu_tls_pin_error` — the pin was checked and did not match — which is a
different class from "cannot pin". `?zuhttp_tls` has the table for every
platform.

### Public-key pinning

A pin says: whatever the certificate chain, the server's key must be this
one. It is checked in addition to normal verification, never instead of it.
The pin is the SHA-256 of the server's public key, and `openssl` computes it:

```{r pin}
pin <- system2("sh", c("-c", shQuote(paste(
  "openssl x509 -in", f("leaf.pem"), "-pubkey -noout |",
  "openssl pkey -pubin -outform der |",
  "openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | openssl base64 -A"))), stdout = TRUE)
pin <- paste0("sha256//", pin)

if ("pins" %in% zu_info()$tls_capabilities) {
  zu_resp_status(zu_get(site, tls = zu_tls(ca_extra = ca, pins = pin)))
} else {
  "pinning is not available on this platform yet"
}
```

## Turning verification off

`verify = FALSE` disables certificate and hostname checks for a request or a
client. It exists for local development against a self-signed server; with
it, anyone between you and the server can read and change the traffic.

```{r insecure}
zu_resp_status(zu_get(site, verify = FALSE))
```

Prefer `ca_extra` with the development server's certificate: it is one more
line and keeps verification on.

## When the platform blocks a certificate

Sometimes a certificate authority has to stop being trusted faster than a
release cycle allows, and sometimes only part of one: an intermediate whose
key leaked, under a root the rest of the web still relies on. A list of
trusted roots, which is what a CA bundle file is, has no way to say "trust
this root but not that intermediate". A platform's trust evaluator can, and
on macOS zuhttp asks it.

In October 2026 eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates turned out to have
private keys anyone could recover ([the disclosure, with test
hosts](https://emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/)). Firefox and Chrome blocked
them on 17 October, Microsoft on 20 October and Apple on 22 October. Each test
host serves a chain through them; a refusal is the safe answer. Measured on 30
October 2026 with zuhttp 0.1.0 and the `curl` package:

| Machine | TLS in zuhttp | zuhttp | `curl` package |
|---|---|---|---|
| macOS 15.7, with Apple's update | Network.framework, `SecTrust` | refused all 4: "certificate is blocked" | connected to all 4 (LibreSSL, `/etc/ssl/cert.pem`) |
| macOS 26.6 runner, with the update | Network.framework, `SecTrust` | refused all 4: "certificate is blocked" | connected to all 4 |
| macOS 26.6 runner, without it | Network.framework, `SecTrust` | connected to 2; refused the 2 never logged for CT: "certificate is not standards compliant" | connected to all 4 |
| Ubuntu 24.04 runner | OpenSSL, distribution bundle | refused all 4: issuer not found | refused all 4: issuer not found |
| Windows build 26100 runner, without Microsoft's block | Schannel | connected to all 4 | connected to all 4 |

The four hosts cover the chain directly under the eMudhra root, the one
cross-signed by Sectigo's AAA root, and a version of each whose certificate
was never logged for Certificate Transparency. The two macOS runners report
the same OS version: Apple delivers a block like this one as an update to its
trust data, and one runner had received it and the other had not. On macOS:

```r
u <- "https://dv-g3b-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/"
tryCatch(zu_get(u), zu_tls_certificate_error = conditionMessage)
#> [1] "certificate verification failed for 'dv-g3b-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com': “dv-g3b-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com” certificate is blocked"
```

That refusal needs no configuration: `zu_info()$revocation_default` is
`FALSE`, and what refused the chain is the platform's block list, not a
revocation check. Nor does the Certificate Transparency refusal: Apple's
evaluator requires a publicly trusted certificate to have been logged, and
zuhttp asks that evaluator.

What this does not show. On Linux, zuhttp trusts the distribution's bundle, a
file that can drop a root but cannot block an intermediate; Ubuntu refused
here only because the bundle lacks these hosts' issuer. On Windows the block
reaches Schannel through the same kind of update, which the runner measured
here had not received. zuhttp checks no Certificate Transparency of its own,
so a client of the platform evaluator is as good as that evaluator, and as
current as the machine's trust data, and no better. The hosts are a record of one
incident and will not be up for ever; `tools/check-trust-blocks.R` in the
source repository repeats the measurement while they are.

## Revocation

Certificate revocation is **not** checked by default, on any platform —
`zu_info()$revocation_default` says so. Checking it costs an extra network
round trip inside the platform's trust code, which zuhttp cannot time out or
cancel. `zu_tls(revocation = TRUE)` asks for it where the platform can do it
(macOS and Windows); OpenSSL has no revocation source of its own and refuses.

## Proxies

HTTPS through a proxy uses `CONNECT`: the proxy relays encrypted bytes and
never sees the content, so certificate checks are between you and the real
server, exactly as without one. The [proxies article](proxies.html) has
worked examples.

```{r cleanup, include = FALSE}
srv$stop()
unlink(d, recursive = TRUE)
```
